title: God's back (Exodus 33:18–23)
hookLine: Moses hidden in a cleft of rock sees God pass by

lines: AFTER THE CALF, ONE MORE REQUEST.
cards: After the calf and the broken tablets, Moses makes one more request, and it's a bold one. He has spoken with God in the cloud and heard the voice.
Now he asks in four words, as the Douay-Rheims has it: "Shew me thy glory." Not a sign, not a plan, not help with the people. Just: let me see you.
And God says yes, and also no.

teach.b: First, the yes. God says: I'll make all my goodness pass before you, and I'll call out my name. Second, the no.
"Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me and live." Here's the strange part.

teach.h: NO ONE SEES MY FACE AND LIVES.
teach.b: Earlier in this same chapter, the text says God spoke to Moses face to face, the way a man speaks to his friend. So which is it? The Bible holds both: real closeness, real conversation, and still a limit.
Third, the rock. God says: stand on the rock by me.

teach.h: A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.
teach.b: When my glory passes, I'll put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I've gone by. Then I'll take my hand away, "and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face thou canst not see."
The Hebrew word is achorai, my back, what's behind me, after me. Moses sees God only from behind, only as God is going past. Fourth, what Catholic writers made of it.
Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, said that seeing God's back means following him: you see the back of someone you walk behind.

Some readers find a version of this in their own lives: they rarely notice grace in the moment, and see its shape only afterward, looking back. The Church teaches that seeing God face to face is the promise of heaven.
Paul says it in a line: we see now through a glass in a dark manner, but then face to face.
And centuries later, on another mountain, the Gospels put Moses beside Jesus at the Transfiguration, looking at a face that shines like the sun.

how: Some Catholics pray the examen at night, looking back over the day to notice where God was present, a practice taught by Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and the Church teaches that seeing God face to face is the joy of heaven.

games.q: you're Moses. you've just asked to see God's glory. God says yes, but no one can see God's face and live. what does God do?
o: shows his face anyway, just once.
hides you in a cleft of the rock and lets you see his back.
games.why: God places him in a cleft, covers him with a hand as the glory passes, then lets him see from behind.

practice: Pick one hard stretch of your life that's over now, or mostly over, and walk back through it slowly, without reliving it: who showed up that you didn't expect, what door opened, what small mercy did you barely notice at the time?
If you pray, thank God for one thing you only see now; if not, simply name what carried you.

wordCard.voice: God's back. What Moses saw from a cleft in the rock: God's glory passing by, seen only from behind. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: my back, what is behind me. what Moses is allowed to see in Exodus 33:23.

carryVoice: Your line: seen from behind. Some things are clearest once they've passed. See you tomorrow.
